canberra.title: Clayface is as terrifying and brutal as comic book movies get
canberra.snippet: Comic book movies based on supervillains very rarely work. With the exception of Joaquin Phoenix’s first Joker film, most are shall...
canberra.content:
Clayface is based on the DC supervillain of the same name and is the newest movie in the superhero franchise. Photo: Warner Bros.

Comic book movies based on supervillains very rarely work.

With the exception of Joaquin Phoenix’s first Joker film, most are shallow, mediocre outings released to make a quick buck.

Since 2017, we’ve had three Venom films, none of which were great. Kraven, which is somehow worse and Morbius, which, if you haven’t seen it, consider yourself blessed.

With the track record of supervillain movies being rocky, to say the least, you’d have to be very ambitious or greedy to pull from that well again, right?

But despite being only two movies deep into their brand-new comic book universe, DC Studios thought it was worth the risk, so we have a new horror movie based on the obscure Batman villain Clayface.

Clayface follows Matt Hagan (Tom Rhys Harries), a Gotham City actor who celebrates recently winning an Academy Award by hitting the club. Matt meets Mia Torrez (Joana Ribeiro), the girlfriend of feared mob boss Markos Szabo (David Dencik).

Even after being warned about her criminal links, Matt spends the night with Mia. An enraged Markos then gets payback by disfiguring Matt’s face with a knife.

Left scarred, Matt is desperate to return to his life of fame and fortune. He turns to a new and untested experimental procedure that allows him to repair his face.

While it initially seems successful, things quickly get worse, and Matt’s skin slowly turns into a clay-like substance. Now angry and mangled but with new abilities, Matt decides to instead hunt down those who wronged him.

As a film, in a word, Clayface is brutal.

Unlike almost every superhero movie I’ve ever seen, Clayface uses its MA rating to deliver a truly violent, gory and unpleasant experience. A particular moment set in a bathroom on an aeroplane will sit with me for weeks.

These moments make the film stand out and separate it from other films in the genre. It doesn’t try to redeem its main character like other villain-focused films do, and it’s not interested in being kid-friendly.

Unfortunately, the movie’s narrative doesn’t match the quality of its gross-out moments. Harries is great as Matt, and he does well with the script he’s given, but there’s only so much he can do with a very standard revenge story.

This makes the movie more of an experience than a film. Audiences will see Clayface, cover their eyes, scream out loud and do their best not to squirm in a cinema, but they won’t revisit it once they’ve seen it.

At the movie’s best, it’s a comic-book version of 2024’s The Substance and David Cronenberg’s The Fly. At its worst, it’s a run-of-the-mill revenge plot, like a straight-to-streaming action flick.

For the most part, the visual gags are horrifically fantastic. It really does create the feeling that this man is slowly turning to mush. They make the movie truly worth watching, if you can stomach it.

The score is also pretty solid, and the production really makes the underbelly of the famous Gotham City pop.

It’s worth touching on where Batman fits into all of this. DC Studios has confirmed he is in the universe and Gotham is his home. However, there is no mention of him throughout the movie.

Fans who want the Caped Crusader to come up against Matt should temper their expectations, because it doesn’t happen here.

All these factors make for a slightly above-average horror outing.

The gore and the horror elements are very strong and Harries is a very entertaining lead. The faults are solely script-based.

If you want horror, Clayface is worth the price of admission. If you’re after something a little deeper, maybe wait until it hits HBO Max in the new year.

Clayface is showing in cinemas now.

canberra.title: 57 deaths, 20-day median: What Canberra’s first assisted dying report reveals
canberra.snippet: For someone nearing the end of their life even a short journey to a doctor’s appointment can be an ordeal. Yet in Canberra, people ...
canberra.content:
The ACT government has marked one year of voluntary assisted dying, with new figures showing 57 people accessed the scheme in its first eight months. Photo: Palliative Care Australia.

For someone nearing the end of their life even a short journey to a doctor’s appointment can be an ordeal. Yet in Canberra, people seeking voluntary assisted dying may still have to travel for consultations that could otherwise take place over the phone or by video.

It is one of the biggest barriers remaining one year after the ACT introduced voluntary assisted dying, with new figures revealing that 57 Canberrans died through the scheme in its first eight months.

The ACT Voluntary Assisted Dying Oversight Board’s inaugural report, released this week (3 November), shows 163 people made an initial request between 3 November 2025 and 30 June 2026.

Of those, 156 underwent a first assessment, 128 had a consulting assessment, 116 made a second request and 110 reached the final request stage.

Approved substances were dispensed in 65 cases, with 57 deaths recorded following administration. The median age of people making an initial request was 77, while the median time between a first request and death was just 20 days.

However, the numbers do not necessarily represent people who abandoned or were refused access to the scheme. Some were still progressing through the process when the reporting period ended.

The oversight board, which reviews cases after they are completed, found no systemic safety concerns during the reporting period.

But while the ACT Government celebrated the first anniversary of the scheme, officials acknowledged that access remains difficult for some of the people it is intended to help.

Attorney-General Tara Cheyne said Commonwealth criminal laws restricting certain voluntary assisted dying conversations over telecommunications were creating unnecessary hardship.

The restrictions stem from federal laws introduced more than two decades ago to address suicide-related material communicated electronically. Ms Cheyne argued those provisions should not prevent medical practitioners from discussing lawful voluntary assisted dying with patients.

For someone who was seriously ill, she said, the inability to have certain conversations remotely could cause considerable distress. Even in a relatively small jurisdiction such as Canberra, travelling to appointments can be difficult for people approaching the end of their lives.

Oversight board chair Darlene Cox agreed that the restrictions were a significant obstacle.

“There’s a lot of public discussion around rural and remote areas, but when you’re at end of life, when you are very unwell, it’s actually very challenging to get to appointments,” she said.

Ms Cheyne said state and territory ministers had been pressing the Commonwealth to address the issue, with further discussions expected at the next meeting of attorneys-general.

The figures also raise questions about the availability of medical professionals willing and trained to participate. According to the report, 43 practitioners completed mandatory training during the first eight months.

Asked whether the existing workforce was sufficient to meet demand, Health Minister Marisa Paterson said the government was continuing to encourage more practitioners to become involved.

“We are always looking for more clinicians who would like to be involved in supporting the community through voluntary assisted dying,” she said.

Unlike some other Australian jurisdictions, the ACT does not require a person to be within a specified timeframe of death to qualify, although strict eligibility criteria apply.

There are also no mandatory waiting periods between the stages of the process and nurse practitioners can undertake assessments as authorised practitioners.

Dr Paterson said the government was proud of the scheme’s first year but acknowledged further work was needed. One unresolved issue involves people who have been approved for voluntary assisted dying but subsequently lose the capacity to make decisions.

Under the current framework, maintaining decision-making capacity is an important requirement for accessing the scheme.

The ACT Government is preparing a citizens’ jury to consider how the law should respond when an eligible person has clearly expressed a wish to access assisted dying but loses capacity before completing the process.

The jury’s recommendations could shape future changes to the legislation, with a broader review scheduled for 2028.

Meanwhile, Palliative Care ACT has called for better integration between palliative care and voluntary assisted dying, rather than treating them as competing options.

Chief executive officer Paul Arztenhofer said the anniversary provided an opportunity to examine how patients, families and health professionals could be better supported. He also called for stronger support for the palliative care workforce.

canberra.title: The more I learn, the less I know: Expanding my viewpoint exposed chasms of ignorance
canberra.snippet: I attended the Blue Mountains Writers Festival in Katoomba last weekend and estimate I am 78 per cent smarter for the experience. I’m def...
canberra.content:
Benjamin Law and Michael Mohammed Admad helped make Haylet at least 78 per cent smarter. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

I attended the Blue Mountains Writers Festival in Katoomba last weekend and estimate I am 78 per cent smarter for the experience.

I’m definitely feeling brighter, in any case.

Not a natural scholar, my university experience felt more like learning by osmosis. I flitted in and out of classes between bar crawls, music festivals and the multiple jobs I had to work to support such a lifestyle.

Now, all grown up, it was a treat to dive into an intensive learning environment. But in doing so, I uncovered cavernous holes in my knowledge. I approached with intrigue.

My first session immediately set the scene for a steep learning curve. It was the ABC’s Benjamin Law in conversation with Miles Franklin-shortlisted author Michael Mohammed Ahmad.

Mohammed is an award-winning novelist with a PhD in creative writing, as well as the founding director of Sweatshop Literacy Movement, a not-for-profit organisation supporting writers from Indigenous and non-English-speaking backgrounds.

So – shock me – he was a fountain of knowledge. For me, he was also a window to other worlds. My experience as an audience member was effectively one long ‘Aha!’ moment. I’m still absorbing half of what was shared.

One particularly mind-expanding realisation was about the relationship between language and our perception of reality.

Known as ‘linguistic relativity’, it refers to how language can influence how its speakers think, perceive and move through the world.

To illustrate his point, Mohammed showed how Arabic identifies cousin relationships with great specificity, detailing parental, sibling and gender lineage. He contrasted that with other cultures that use much broader language around family.

He drew a fascinating line between these linguistics and different cultural approaches to the ‘acceptability’ of marriage within family lines.

As an English speaker, this blew my monolingual mind.

I looked around the room with interest, wondering what parallel universes of understanding were among us.

Whipping out my phone, I did some quick research and found several examples.

Russian features distinct words for light and dark blue, and research suggests its speakers distinguish such shades faster than English speakers.

Here in Australia, the Indigenous Guugu Yimithirr language uses north/south/east/west rather than ‘left/right’, with many positing that this helps speakers maintain a continuous sense of orientation.

When accidents occur, English tends to emphasise who caused the problem – John broke the vase – whereas Japanese speakers are more inclined to focus on the event – the vase broke – often leaving the human out entirely.

As a vase-breaker from way back, I appreciate this grammatical trickery.

A first-hand example comes to mind in the way Spanish treats age.

While I consider myself an English-only speaker, I did gain a half-decent grasp of Spanish for a time, when travelling in South America.

In English, I am 40 years old. It has permanence. It is a state of my being.

In Spanish, the phrase is ‘Tengo 40 años’, which literally translates as ‘I have 40 years’. Age is something I have accumulated, not what I am.

Another tick from me!

A word of warning on this Spanish phrase. It should not be confused with ‘Tengo 40 anos’, which carries a completely different, anatomical meaning. A lesson I unfortunately learnt in casual conversation with a small Peruvian child, whose version of reality was forever altered.

Sometimes it’s the absence of words which influences us.

Back at the festival, Pip Williams, author of The Dictionary of Lost Words, The Bookbinder of Jericho and now The German Ward, touched on how things that go unrecorded can impact our understanding of history.

In fact, her debut novel was inspired by the word “bondmaid” (a female slave forced to serve without wages) and its exclusion from the first edition of the Oxford English Dictionary.

My mind spun as I grappled with our vulnerable history books and the unperceived truths beyond my reach. As the saying goes, “You don’t know what you don’t know”.

Overall, my enlightening weekend was a good reminder that – among the rhythms and routines of our daily grind – it’s easy to fall into an echo chamber.

Or less “fall”, more “sink gradually, without realising”.

Daily life keeps us busy, often moving through familiar spaces and having familiar conversations with familiar faces.

For my part, I’m going to make more of an effort to crawl out of my comfortable chamber and seek new horizons.

Because I left the festival feeling decidedly smarter – or at least, more aware of how little I know.

canberra.title: 6 reasons to love Sapling Yard’s new cellar door (hint: they’re all wine)
canberra.snippet: It’s been a big year for local boutique winery Sapling Yard. Founder and winemaker Carla Rodeghiero (along with her co-winemaker Malcolm ...
canberra.content:
The Sapling Yard Cellar Door is a lovely spot to enjoy a tasting in the sun with snacks from neighbouring Aranya Acres. Photo: Martin Conway.

It’s been a big year for local boutique winery Sapling Yard.

Founder and winemaker Carla Rodeghiero (along with her co-winemaker Malcolm Burdett) picked up a trophy at the National Wine Show earlier this year and have now shifted their cellar door to be co-located with their winemaking facilities out at Aranya Acres.

I had visited the Aranya Acres restaurant (formerly the site of Contentious Character) at Wamboin shortly after they opened. The Sapling Yard Cellar door feels appropriately ‘cellar-ish’, tucked under the main restaurant building.

Visiting on a sunny Saturday, the dappled shade in the courtyard formed the perfect backdrop for a tasting. We were given the option of low tables or high-top bars and decided to perch on stools at a wine barrel.

The standard tasting is 6 glasses. You can choose your own drops, or have the staff pick for you. We let the lovely Rachelle guide us, and we’re glad we did.

Get yourself a grazing board and settle in for a great afternoon. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

But first: snacks.

The antipasto board on offer here is a serious affair: gorgeous squid-ink salami, oozy soft cheese, fiery ‘nduja salami, olives, pickled fennel, and some juicy figs. Absolutely spot on, and totally delicious.

The cellar door menu comes from the Aranya Acres kitchen, and you can also enjoy oysters, sardines and something called ‘ultimate garlic bread’ that sounds utterly vampire-proof.

To start, Rachelle poured us a taste of the Entrachet, a sparkling wine made in the classic Champagne style. Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Meunier grapes are used for this wine, which is left ‘on lees’ (in contact with yeast residue) for 18 months. This lets the wine develop those toasty brioche flavours you’d expect in a Champagne. It’s dry, refreshing and oh-so-drinkable on a hot day!

At this point in our tasting, we were visited by the local wildlife: a fellow diner initially warned us of a snake moving our way, but it turned out to be a friendly (and fat!) blue tongue lizard.

Sapling Yard winemakers Malcolm Burdett and Carla Rodeghiero won a trophy at the National Wine Show for their Fiori wine. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

Our only request for the tasting was for a Riesling – to quote my plus-one, “I’d kill for a cheeky Riesling right about now!”. To avoid any wine-related homicides, Rachelle happily complied.

Made with grapes from Lake George, this wine is everything you want from a Canberra region Riesling. Dry, acidic, refreshing and full of punchy lime and green apple notes, with just a touch of blossom.

Speaking of blossom: up next we tasted the Fiori, the white blend that won Sapling Yard their trophy.

I’ve had this wine before, and every time I am delighted by the perfume of this delicate drop. Gewürztraminer grapes add a musky, sticky sweetness, while Pinot Gris adds crisp pear, and Pinot Blanc and Riesling balance everything out with a little citric acidity. It’s unique, really delicious and an absolute bargain at $32 a bottle.

We rounded out the tasting with a few reds.

The Shiraz Viognier – a wine I always associate with Canberra region makers – is a top-notch example of the style. The Gamay and Montepulciano were both bold and flavourful, but still light enough to enjoy on a hot day.

Each of the six wines we tasted was either a perfect example of its style, or a whole new expression of what Canberra Region wines can be. For my money, Carla is making some of the region’s best wines.

We rounded out our visit with a wander through some creative bird statues on the lawns. You can also book a full tour of the winery if you’d like a behind-the-scenes peek at how things are done.

Sapling Yard Cellar Door is located at 810 Norton Road, Wamboin, adjacent to Aranya Acres restaurant. They are open for tastings on Saturday from 11 am to 5 pm and Sunday from 12 pm to 4 pm. Reservations are recommended (especially if you’d like a tour). Follow Sapling Yard on Facebook or Instagram.

canberra.title: Petrol or plug-in hybrid? We compare two similar but very different Mitsubishi Outlanders
canberra.snippet: Same age. Same income. Same starting balance. The difference? One Mitsubishi Outlander in this seemingly identical pair packs a perfectly...
canberra.content:
8 November 2026

Join the conversation

5

Although they look almost identical, the PHEV (left) and petrol (right) versions of the Mitsubishi Outlander deliver vastly different experiences. Photo: Mitsubishi Motors Australia (edited with AI).

Same age. Same income. Same starting balance. The difference? One Mitsubishi Outlander in this seemingly identical pair packs a perfectly conventional petrol engine, while the other is a thrifty plug-in hybrid.

But just how do these two fuel types compare? In the ACT, and indeed across Australia, plug-in hybrids are the least popular type of new vehicle sold.

However, PHEV sales have increased in recent months, while sales of internal combustion engine vehicles are going downhill.

Some will argue that opting for a PHEV is a bit like being a fence-sitter; it screams, “I wanted an EV but have too much range anxiety”.

It’s a solution I’ve long been a fan of, though – so long as you understand how to get the best out of a PHEV, which does require more thought.

To compare the pair and see whether it really makes sense for more buyers to switch from pure petrol to a PHEV, I spent time in two almost identical Mitsubishi Outlanders.

Why the Outlander? In 2014, the previous-generation model was the first plug-in hybrid SUV to be sold in Australia. It was also the first PHEV I ever drove, and the first to offer a glimpse of its genuine future viability.

That future, clearly, is now.

The petrol Outlander got a facelift in 2025, which carried over to the PHEV model in 2026. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

What is it?

The Mitsubishi Outlander doesn’t need much of an introduction. It’s consistently been one of the best-selling SUVs in the country, and among the top-sellers in any category.

It recently received a number of commendable changes to freshen it up, including a new suspension and steering setup honed on the roads of South Australia to better suit Aussie conditions.

For this comparison, we’ve got the one you really want: the top-spec Outlander Exceed Tourer, finished in Moonstone Grey with lavish brick brown semi-aniline leather.

Whatever on earth semi-aniline means, I can tell you it’s very lovely.

The Exceed Tourer scores the best upgrades. A set of baller 20-inch diamond-cut alloys complement the Outlander’s refreshed looks, with revised bumpers and smoked rear tail-lights.

Inside, you’ll now find a bangin’ 12-speaker premium Yamaha audio system that’s among the best out there, which has been added to a cabin that already featured luxuries as extensive as massage seats. Yep, in a humble Mitsi!

Mind you, this Mitsubishi isn’t so humble when it comes to the price tag.

The conventional petrol model packs a 2.5-litre four-pot that serves up 135kW. With standard all-wheel drive in this spec, it asks for $57,990 before on-road costs.

In the top-spec Outlander Exceed Tourer on test here, you’ll find a gorgeous brick brown leather interior. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

By contrast, the PHEV offers over 63 per cent more power from its 221kW hybrid system, utilising a 2.4-litre engine and two electric motors. However, it commands a $74,490 price tag – a 28 per cent price jump.

The savings are promised through a drastic reduction in fuel consumption. The petrol’s 8.1L/100km claim falls to just 1.2L/100km for the PHEV. My testing revealed 8.6L/100km and 1.9L/100km in the real world, respectively.

At the average Canberra fuel price of 206.5 cents a litre, the dearest in the country during Q3 2026 according to FuelRadar, it will take over 115,000 km of driving to break even on the price difference between them – and that’s before factoring the additional cost of charging.

The upside is that the Outlander PHEV has an impressive 103 km of electric-only driving range – a claim which isn’t too far-fetched.

Despite their vastly different underpinnings, there aren’t many ways to tell the two apart, aside from the extra badging on the PHEV’s boot and front doors.

The only other change is there being a filler flap on both sides of the PHEV model. Weirdly, the petrol filler even moves from the right side to the left, while the flap on the right side is bigger. Producing four totally different rear quarter panels can’t be too cheap.

Additional badging on the doors and boot lid are one of the only ways to tell the PHEV apart. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Badging across the bonnet... just like a Range Rover. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

20-inch alloys are standard on this top-spec model. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

The Outlander PHEV accepts both Type 2 and CHAdeMO chargers. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Additional badging on the doors and boot lid are one of the only ways to tell the PHEV apart. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

From a low-enough angle, you might spot the battery pack underneath the Outlander PHEV. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Blink and you'll miss the differences on this petrol model when compared to the PHEV. Photo: Mitsubishi Motors Australia.

The Outlander now features a local suspension and steering tune, developed on the roads of South Australia. Photo: Mitsubishi Motors Australia.

The Outlander PHEV uses a 2.4-litre engine with two electric motors, delivering a healthy 221kW. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

What’s it like to live with?

If there’s one thing that’s $16,500 better about the Outlander PHEV, it’s the way it drives.

The regular-degular petrol model has been vastly improved thanks to the new, localised suspension setup. It’s a pretty sweet thing to steer.

But the PHEV, thanks to its additional weight and lower centre of gravity, is even better. It simply feels more settled on the road, and even a bit more premium than the already impressive ‘normal’ model. There’s a reason our subconscious associates heavier things with being more luxurious.

The PHEV is also far punchier thanks to its instant electric power, and far smoother thanks to how those electric motors deliver it.

To really extract the most out of the PHEV, though, you’ll need to put your thinking cap on, rather than simply getting in and sliding the leather-clad shifter into D.

Between the shifter and drive mode dial, the PHEV has two extra buttons. The one on the left turns on one-pedal driving, which ramps up regenerative braking, so it should come to a stop without using the brake pedal.

The other button, marked ‘EV’, is the one you’ll really need to pay attention to. For most people, leaving it in Normal mode will be fine, especially in a place like Canberra. If you have a longer commute or plan on taking a road trip, however, you might want to play around with it.

The front seats offer heating, ventilation, and even massage functions. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

The rear seats are also heated. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

There are three different seat massage programs to choose from, with different intensity levels. Photo: Mitsubishi Motors Australia.

The Yamaha premium audio system is among the best out there. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

In addition to seven drive modes, there is also one-pedal driving and four powertrain configurations to choose from. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Instead of a tachometer, the PHEV model gets a gauge that shows regenerative braking, EV power, and petrol power usage. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

There are four powertrain settings: Normal, EV, Save, and Charge. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Put it into Save when you’re on a freeway or long country road, and it will run the petrol engine (which operates more efficiently than an electric motor at high speeds) and preserve your battery charge for city streets.

When you get there, pop it into EV mode, and it will use the electric motors in their most efficient environment, instead of keeping a petrol engine idling pointlessly.

If you forget to do either and leave it in Normal, it will churn through a battery charge on the freeway; there’s even a Charge mode that uses the petrol engine like a generator to top the battery back up.

A little bit of thought goes a long way.

The verdict

There’s little question in my mind, at least, that the PHEV is the better Outlander of the two tested here. Smoother, more powerful, far more efficient. No qualms there.

Whether it’s worth the extra cost comes down not only to how you plan to use it, but how long you plan to keep it.

If you know you’ll keep this thing for a while – worth doing with Mitsubishi offering up to 10 years of warranty coverage if you service at an authorised dealership – then you’ll make back those savings by the time you come to upgrade.

It’s also worth keeping in mind that while novated leasing deals for PHEVs like the Outlander have been exempt from fringe benefits tax, there are increasing calls for this subsidy scheme to be scrapped at the time of writing.

However, if you’re the sort of person who upgrades your car regularly, you simply won’t see a return on those savings unless you’re on the open road all day, where the PHEV makes less sense anyway.

In a place like Canberra, though, going PHEV – regardless of what vehicle you’re looking at – makes an awful lot of sense. Thrifty around the roundabouts, yet (almost) thought-free on a drive up to Sydney.

While the petrol Outlander is significantly cheaper than the equivalent PHEV model, each version is clearly suited to a different type of buyer. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

2026 Mitsubishi Outlander Exceed Tourer Petrol

  • $57,990 before on-road costs
  • 2.5-litre four-cylinder, 135 kW/244 Nm
  • CVT, all-wheel drive
  • 8.1 litres per 100km, 55-litre fuel capacity
  • 1695 kg kerb weight.

2026 Mitsubishi Outlander Exceed Tourer PHEV

  • $74,990 before on-road costs
  • 2.4-litre four-cylinder with two electric motors, 221 kW
  • CVT, all-wheel drive
  • 1.2 litres per 100km, 53-litre fuel capacity
  • 103 km electric range, 22.7 kWh battery pack
  • 2158 kg kerb weight.

Thanks to Mitsubishi Motors Australia for providing this vehicle for testing. Region has no commercial arrangement with Mitsubishi Motors Australia.

australia.title: The cautionary tale of Beck O’Connor … and a government accused of using ‘threatening’ tactics to silence critics
australia.snippet: When Queensland’s first independent victims’ commissioner spoke out, the LNP’s next move was calculated and brutal. Community groups now ...
australia.content:
Queensland’s first independent victims’ commissioner, Beck O’Connor, found herself in the crosshairs of a new Liberal National party government that had staked its future on a promise to serve the interests of victims of crime. In the government’s first nine months, O’Connor made a few mild and reasoned criticisms of its hardline crime plans.

On the signature “adult crime, adult time” measure she said advancing victims’ rights “should not be to the detriment of universal human rights”. She then called plans to allow police to issue year-long domestic violence orders “an experiment with unintended but not unforeseen harmful consequences to our community”.

In July last year came a final straw. The government released crime statistics it said were a “transparency boost” on victim numbers. O’Connor sent out a media release – which has been since scrubbed from the commissioner’s website – suggesting that the statistics did not reflect the reality for victims, criticising the lack of baseline numbers and calling for an independent authority on crime data.

The government’s next move was calculated and brutal. It leaked an unreleased report into DV Connect, the support service where O’Connor had previously been chief executive, to the Courier-Mail. Amanda Camm, then the state minister for the prevention of domestic and family violence, used parliamentary privilege to claim that O’Connor had “caused significant damage to the relationship and trust between the service and our government”. The premier, David Crisafulli, told a press conference she had “questions to answer”.

It is unclear who leaked the government reports and whether Camm or Crisafulli was aware of them.

O’Connor denied any claim of wrongdoing or impropriety but the leaks to journalists continued. She resigned a few weeks later.

“When it looks like the government is targeting people who engage in reasonable debate it puts a chill across the whole sector,” says Katherine Hayes, the chief executive officer of the Youth Advocacy Centre, another organisation that has been critical of the government’s agenda.

Last week Yac had funding for its successful bail support program slashed.

The state government now faces accusations of using “threatening” tactics to silence its critics. In interviews with more than 20 people, current and former government officials, community sector workers and others describe a systematic campaign to suppress public criticism of its policies.

They accused the government of creating a “culture of fear” and overreach in the community sector, particularly in the areas of youth justice and child safety where the government is reliant on service providers including residential care agencies to enact state programs.

Several also raised concern about the way the government has scrapped, neutered or politicised notionally independent oversight mechanisms that are supposed to provide a check on state power.

Put in the ‘naughty corner’

Several people who spoke to Guardian Australia recounted “belligerent” or dismissive interactions with some ministerial staff. The head of a not-for-profit organisation says staffers appear uninterested in listening and “will just come in and tell us everything needs to change”.

Another said: “The government doesn’t have a mature approach. A properly functioning government does consultation when they’re developing their ideas or solutions and listens to criticism.”

When the government’s hand-picked panel of gender-based violence victim survivors made recommendations – including for police reforms – that ultimately clashed with the government’s agenda, the findings were buried. One woman, dissatisfied with the response, was told she was no longer welcome to phone the minister’s offices.

Community groups have claimed, as first reported in the Courier-Mail, direct government threats to cut funding if they spoke out about the LNP and its policies.

The director of a residential care provider, Nicole Hague, said her service had been put in the “naughty corner” by the state government after she was quoted in the Courier-Mail as the author of a letter accusing the government of treating vulnerable children “as a balance-sheet deficit to be trimmed”.

Since speaking out, she says, referrals to her service by the government have dried up, despite a well-documented statewide shortage of places in residential care.

Hague says her service is now in financial trouble “because we advocate for our kids”.

“I was told if I spoke out that they would target me,” she says. “Providers are just trying to protect kids, and our funding is what we need to do that.”

Hayes says she had had two separate discussions “with former ministerial advisers who had indicated that ministerial offices weren’t happy with speaking out”.

Last week Labor tabled documents in parliament showing residential care providers had been made to sign a “confidentiality agreement” to bid for new contracts, including a prohibition on taking legal action against the state.

“We know that this government is very afraid of people taking action against them and speaking out against them,” she said.

“And I think Queenslanders deserve some answers, as do residential care providers, about why they are being prohibited from taking [legal] action.”

The child safety minister, Amanda Stoker, told parliament that the government had “done more to bring into the sunshine the reality of the difficult lives these young people have faced” than Labor had in its near decade in government.

Truth telling

Another cause for concern in Queensland is the diminished influence of “independent statutory authorities” and officials whose job is often to scrutinise and provide a check on government plans.

The government has scrapped some of these roles, including that of the former First Nations co-commissioner at the Queensland Family and Child Commission, the respected advocate Natalie Lewis. The office of the independent implementation coordinator – responsible for publishing progress reports on recommendations to address gender-based violence and police reform – was scrapped last year.

Guardian Australia and the ABC have previously reported claims of a “project invisibility” that has removed First Nations voices, particularly outspoken ones, from government roles.

The government’s first act after its election in 2024 was to end a First Nations “truth telling and healing” inquiry. One former government official says while reaction rightly focused on implications for First Nations issues and reconciliation, the move was “a broader signal that truth telling was no longer something the government would tolerate”.

Scott McDougall, the former human rights commissioner, had repeatedly raised human rights concerns about legislation, including during the term of the former Labor government. In his place the government chose a former police officer, Debbie Platz, who began her tenure saying she wanted to be “collaborative” rather than “combative”.

In a submission to a review of Queensland’s human rights framework, McDougall said Queensland’s parliament, which has no upper house, gave the government “carte blanche” to pass laws.

“Without a house of review, a system of scrutinising bills of parliament for impact on human rights becomes essential,” McDougall wrote.

“It would be fair to say that the existing committee system is not working effectively to prevent significant infringements on human rights.”

In lieu of an upper house, the Queensland parliament subjects proposed legislation to a committee review process, which includes public hearings. Increasingly during this term of parliament, the government-controlled committees have chosen not to invite critics or opponents of government plans to give evidence.

‘An essential part of democracy’

Most of the people who spoke to Guardian Australia were unwilling to speak publicly due to concerns about backlash, potential damage to relationships or the prospect of cuts to funding.

Many brought up the treatment of O’Connor unprompted, describing the government’s attack on her as “coordinated and brutal” and that it had made people afraid of consequences if they spoke out.

O’Connor was approached but did not want to comment.

“What happened with Beck O’Connor is always in my mind when I’m doing public advocacy,” Hayes says.

“What she said was always evidence-based, factual and reasonable. I had always thought that engaging in that level of debate would be respected, rather than feared.

“It’s always on my mind because the government’s approach is the opposite of reasonable and evidence-based. And we see it as our duty to engage in a public dialogue about that as an essential part of democracy.”

The government has said Yac “was not successful” in its application to continue to run the bail support program in Brisbane and that other organisations were chosen instead.

Hayes says Yac had its funding withdrawn despite meeting and exceeding KPIs for its program. She says the decision to hand the contract to another provider will cause “a huge amount of distress” for young people who have been helped by the program and built important relationships with workers.

Hayes says the funding cut appears to be “because we engage in public advocacy”.

On that front, she says there are now fewer and fewer people willing to challenge the government on its policies, particularly the ever-hardening and populist approach to youth justice.

Parliamentary committee hearings used to feature many voices willing to raise concerns about breaches of human rights, Hayes says, as they did during the Labor government.

“Now it’s just Debbie Kilroy [from Sisters Inside], me and [barrister] Laura Reece. Other than that no one is speaking. Everyone has been silenced.”

A government spokesperson said in response to questions: “inferences made in this unsubstantiated enquiry are firmly rejected”

“After a decade of zero accountability on government service providers, we are setting KPIs for delivery to turn around the crises we inherited across youth crime, health, housing and cost of living.”

australia.title: The Coalition plans to scrap Victoria’s treaty with First Peoples if it wins the election – but is that what voters want?
australia.snippet: Jess Wilson, who once supported the federal Indigenous voice to parliament, has vowed to repeal Victoria’s treaty within the first 100 da...
australia.content:
On a warm Saturday afternoon in the affluent suburb of Kew in Melbourne’s inner-east, three volunteers approach a stately two-storey home armed with a printed page of talking points on Australia’s first-ever treaty with Indigenous peoples. This is one of the most expensive areas in the city, where homes are heavily secured and worth millions. The trio have already been turned away from multiple houses. But this time they are greeted by 26-year-old Paris Riebeling, the first local keen to speak with them.

She opens the door to reveal a large piece of Aboriginal artwork on the wall behind her. She talks about living a privileged life in the “lucky country”.

“It’s always so interesting to be unlearning what living in and growing up in Australia is like,” she says.

Riebeling has lived with her mother and sister in the electorate of Kew since she was a baby. Her local member is the Liberal MP and state opposition leader, Jess Wilson, who has vowed to introduce legislation to repeal Victoria’s treaty with First Nations people within the first 100 days if the Coalition wins the state election on 28 November. One Nation has also pledged to overturn the body.

The state seat of Kew sits within the federal seat of Kooyong, a longtime Liberal party stronghold that has been held by the independent MP Monique Ryan since 2022. It is one of a minority of electorates to have voted in favour of a national Indigenous voice to parliament in the 2023 referendum, with a yes vote of 59%. Wilson was the only Liberal MP in Victoria to publicly support the voice.

It is an affluent, highly educated, predominantly white suburb. But that does not mean treaty is an unimportant issue, Riebeling says. She tells Guardian Australia that issues affecting First Nations peoples are “definitely something that we talk about”.

“I have a lot of privilege and I’m very aware of that,” she says. “I think part of that is acknowledging that, while I didn’t personally do anything, my ancestors did and I benefit from that.”

Checks and balances

Formal discussion around treaty in Victoria began in 2016, with a series of dialogues between traditional owners and Daniel Andrews’s Labor government. The First Peoples’ Assembly of Victoria, an independent and democratically elected body representing traditional owners, was established in 2019, and the Yoorrook Justice Commission, which conducted a statewide truth-telling project, began in 2021. Last November, the historic Statewide Treaty Act 2025 passed state parliament and established a permanent, statutory First Peoples representative body known as Gellung Warl.

Gellung Warl has the power to make rules on a limited number of matters directly affecting First Nations peoples, including guidelines for trading and sharing existing water entitlements between First Nations groups, appointing a First Nations person to the statewide heritage and Aboriginal heritage councils, and creating cultural safety guidelines that may be voluntarily adopted by non-Indigenous agencies. It does not have the power to veto policy or legislation. The independent treaty authority also assists in the negotiation of other agreements between specific traditional owner groups and the state.

Despite this limited scope, it is the strongest step toward self-determination taken by any Australian government since the creation of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission in 1990. That body was unilaterally abolished in 2005 after allegations of corruption. No such allegations have been made about Gellung Warl.

“The thought of treaty being scrapped in the first 100 days after it took 10 years to create is just completely devastating to me,” says Anna Langford, one of the volunteers door-knocking for advocacy group Together for Treaty, a national grassroots movement dedicated to supporting First Nations truth-telling, self-determination and treaty-making.

“It’s just alarming to me that something so important, that so much care has gone into, could be destroyed and most people might not even know that it was there in the first place or sense the importance of it.”

A few streets over from Riebeling, retiree Geoffrey Jewell says he knows “nothing at all” about Gellung Warl but that he’s in favour of treaty “if it helps to give better conditions for Aboriginals to live in, and helps them better understand our society as well”.

“In other words, talking together,” he says. “I think that’s the way to go forward.”

He adds:“I don’t think denying people were here and have been denied resources for a hundred years or more is it. I see the difficulties for the Europeans at that time [of colonisation] but now we know more, and I’m sure we can get to understand more and accommodate things.

“I mean, we see in America just what a society is like when people are not involved and not taking part, and I don’t want to see that happen in Australia for my children and grandchildren.”

The Coalition argues that scrapping treaty would save the state almost $1bn. A Parliamentary Budget Office report requested by Wilson earlier this year found that repealing the treaty laws would save taxpayers $948.3m over the next 10 years . Labor disputed the figures, saying the report included the costs of various services and programs for First Nations peoples that are separate from treaty.

A Coalition campaign spokesperson said the operating cost of Gellung Warl would be better spent on “practical outcomes in health, education, housing and community safety, not more bureaucracy”.

“Our focus is on delivering practical outcomes that make a real difference to the lives of Victorians. That also includes delivering better outcomes for Aboriginal Victorians,” they said.

Gellung Warl co-chair Djaran Murray-Jackson says the long-term goal for treaty in Victoria is self-determination.

“Treaty is an investment in better outcomes and stronger communities, creating opportunities to grow First Peoples businesses and build economic independence,” he says. “Stronger First Peoples economies mean more jobs, investment and opportunities across Victoria, while helping communities shape their own futures and reducing reliance on government systems that haven’t always worked for them.”

Fellow co-chair Meriki Onus says treaty has become “part of the fabric of Victoria” and that elected Gellung Warl members are answerable and accountable to their communities.

“We’re on track to deliver the first steps in economic empowerment and education for our communities within our first six months, while ensuring First Peoples are leading conversations about the issues that affect our lives,” she says. “That’s the work we’re getting on with.”

Protecting Gellung Warl

A YouGov poll in July, commissioned by the First Nations-led not-for-profit group Common Threads, found 58% of respondents said that scrapping Gellung Warl “is out of touch with their priorities across inner, outer, provincial and rural electorates”.

Common Threads spokesperson Tarneen Onus Browne, a Gunditjmara, Yorta Yorta, Bindal and Meriam woman, says treaty is “not really an issue for the general population”.

“It’s just legislation that affects First Nations people but it’s also an agreement with the state that wants to reset the relationship between First Nations people in Victoria,” she says.

Meanwhile, the Victorian Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (VACCHO) has launched an advertising campaign, calling on voters to “protect” treaty.

Its acting chief executive, Jim O’Shea, says First Nations peoples “fought for generations to create change and build a better future for our children and grandchildren” and supporters of treaty “cannot take this progress for granted”.

“We need to protect what has been achieved and continue building on it, not go backwards,” he says.

australia.title: Weakening AI copyright law will spell ‘disaster for creativity’, global music body warns Albanese
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Head of IFPI says allowing AI companies access to online content would be a ‘huge mistake’ and damage Australia’s reputation G...
australia.content:
Australia weakening copyright protections for AI companies would be “ridiculous and dangerous”, the global peak body for the music recording industry has warned as it watches with concern how the Albanese government responds to big tech’s demands.

While local creatives have raised constitutional issues and threatened political backlash, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), representing recording industry bodies worldwide, said its members were worried about Australia potentially agreeing to demands other nations had rejected.

“Why would Australia do this? Why would a sophisticated, democratic country that has a phenomenal cultural power of its own, choose to make this very odd decision and buy into the promises of a few large AI companies, and throw away their own culture and creativity?” Victoria Oakley, the CEO of IFPI, told Guardian Australia.

“I don’t think Australia wants to be the weakest link in this situation, the one that believed the promises and gave in and threw creativity under the bus on behalf of everyone else. That doesn’t feel very Australian to me.

“You just need one safe harbour, because then you can train on music from anywhere in the world. So this isn’t just about Australian music and Australian culture; it’s about music and culture everywhere.”

Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of policy overhauls around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries were alarmed after AI companies requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.

Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model that would allow it to scrape content unless rights holders signalled an objection.

Large AI companies say they need legal certainty on issues like copyright before making investments in Australia or training their models here.

Oakley said AI companies had made similar proposals in the US, UK and other nations and that Australia should not accept such a bargain.

“I just don’t think it’s true that you will only get investment or growth, or be seen as pro-innovation, if you entirely give in to the demands of AI companies,” Oakley said.

“We’ve been talking to capitals around the world, saying ‘are you seeing what’s going on in Australia?’ We think this is a disaster for creativity.”

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said via a spokesperson last week that the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.

Oakley said she worried about AI and copyright “everywhere”, but feared “Australia appears to be threatening to do something really ridiculous and dangerous.”

She said creative industries worried about “contagion” of copyright relaxation if Australia caved in, and that copyright material from anywhere in the world could be affected.

She declined to speculate on any potential legal or constitutional challenges, as raised by the Australian Recording Industry Association, but said it would be reputational damage to Australia’s standing in the creative world.

“It would be a huge mistake, and I think the prize is not worth what you’re throwing away,” she said.

In recent answers to a parliamentary committee on AI, responding to questions from the independent senator David Pocock about why it couldn’t replicate the kind of deals Spotify had made, OpenAI said the music streaming giant “has a different business, where it primarily transmits un-transformed copyrighted content, so would be expected to license content that it streams”.

But Oakley said music labels had already inked dozens of licensing deals with smaller AI companies around the world.

“It is perfectly possible to license. I’m almost shocked that these words are coming out of the mouths of some of the larger AI companies … We already know how to license music to tech platforms because that’s exactly how Spotify works, or Amazon Music, Apple, or Tidal,” she said.

“You have a ready, willing set of rights holders who want to license with a history of licensing in the streaming world, but also current evidence of licensing to AI firms. Let’s let the market do what it needs to do. Come to us and we’ll make it work.”

australia.title: The ‘Taylor Swift of romantasy’ has a new book. Why are people mad? – Full Story Podcast
australia.snippet: With midnight book launches, record-breaking sales and billions of TikTok views, romantasy has turned into one of the biggest commercial ...
australia.content:
With midnight book launches, record-breaking sales and billions of TikTok views, romantasy has turned into one of the biggest commercial juggernauts propping up modern publishing.

But why are stories combining high fantasy and female-centric erotic romance still dismissed by mainstream culture?

Guardian Australia lifestyle editor Alyx Gorman joins Taylah Strano to unpack the global phenomenon of romantasy and the divisive release of Sarah J Maas’s latest novel

world.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
world.snippet: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and...
world.content:
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

world.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The l...
world.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
world.snippet: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result The African National Congress is on cou...
world.content:
The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.

Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.

Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.

Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

world.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK
world.snippet: Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit A British healthcare ...
world.content:
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.

A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths. It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way.

Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.

In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”

Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.

British health authorities say the risk ⁠to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.

There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, ‌according to the UK Health Security Agency.

world.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
world.snippet: Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts The African National Congress is o...
world.content:
The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.

In Kensington, a diverse Johannesburg suburb that has sustained repeated water and power outages in recent weeks, voters said they wanted to see change. The city is currently led by Dada Morero, the ANC mayor, in coalition with the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the rightwing populist Patriotic Alliance (PA).

“Service delivery is bad, it’s horrible,” said Tshepiso Makotse, 26, a call centre worker. “Water, electricity – everything, basically.”

Makotse said she had split her two votes, casting one for the centre-right Democratic Alliance (DA) local councillor and her party vote for the leftwing uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma. “I just want change,” she said.

Terrence Pieters, a retired boilermaker, said: “The infrastructure in Johannesburg is shot.” He declined to say which party he had voted for, other than it was “one of the offshoots of the DA”.

“I would like to see things get better and great people in charge,” said the 72-year-old. “But … there’s no one party that’s going to take over here. It’s going to be a circus, it’s going to be a coalition.”

Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.

Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.

Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.

The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs in various coalitions across the province’s three metros, including under an ActionSA mayor in Tshwane.

In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.

The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who now leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.

In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the MK party was polling above 40%. Zuma, its 84-year-old leader, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.

The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.

South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.
